title: Join algorithms
lead: Nested-loop, indexed, sort-merge and hash joins with explicit page-I/O assumptions.

sections.title: Nested-loop joins
sections.html:
Join output and accounting assumptions

For every matching pair (r,s), the logical join concatenates attributes from both tuples. Projection later chooses the final columns. Avoiding a Cartesian-product intermediate is an implementation improvement, not a change to which pairs must be produced.

R has M pages and m tuples; S has N pages and n tuples. The source uses M=1000,m=100000,N=500,n=40000. Costs below count input/temporary-page I/O and exclude CPU and final output writes consistently. Intermediate output size can still affect later operators or spills; ignoring final output does not make a many-to-many join’s real cost vanish.

PDF pp. 1–4

Tuple and page nested loops

tupleNL(R,S):
  for r in R:
    for s in S: if predicate(r,s): emit(r,s)
pageNL(R,S):
  for pageR in R:
    for pageS in S:
      compare every tuple pair in pageR and pageS

Tuple NL costs M+mN=50,001,000 I/Os; reversing inputs gives N+nM=40,000,500. Page NL reuses a loaded outer page across all its tuples: M+MN, or 500+500·1000=500,500 with S outside. At 0.1 ms/I/O these are about 1.4 hours versus 50 seconds. Page NL needs three buffers including output.

PDF pp. 5–9

Block nested loops and fitting memory

Use B−2 frames for an outer block, one for inner input and one for output. For every outer block, scan all S and compare its tuples to the block. Cost with R outside is M+ceil(M/(B−2))N; also evaluate the reverse orientation because the ceiling can change the preferred direction.

If the outer fits in B−2 frames, scan each relation once: M+N=1500 I/Os, or 0.15 s in the source timing model. Nested loops permits general predicates, including inequalities; its I/O gain comes from reusing data in memory, not reducing the required logical matches.

PDF pp. 10–11

sections.title: Index nested-loop join
sections.html:
Indexed probes and matching-record fetches

for each r in outer R:
  candidates = matching index lookup on inner S
  for each s in candidates:
    if complete predicate(r,s): emit(r,s)

Cost=M+m·lookupCost. A B+ lookup includes tree descent, matching leaf entries and heap fetches; a hash lookup includes bucket/overflow access and heap fetches. Clustered matches cost roughly their data pages; unclustered matches can cost one fetch per tuple. A matching index must exist or its build cost must be included.

Small outer cardinality and few matches per key favour this method. Equality hash probes cannot directly implement an inequality join; a suitable ordered tree may support its range. Cache reuse and duplicate outer keys can change actual probe cost.

PDF pp. 12–15

sections.title: Sort-merge join
sections.html:
Sort-merge state and source result sequence

sort R and S by join key
while neither input exhausted:
  if R.key < S.key: advance R
  else if S.key < R.key: advance S
  else:
    collect both equal-key groups
    emit every matching pair between the groups
    advance beyond both groups

The source R sorts to 100/Alice,200/Michael,300/Bob,400/John,500/Carrol,600/Daniel,700/Lucia. S sorts to 100/2222/Edinburgh,100/9999/London,200/8888/Oxford,400/6666/London,500/7777/Edinburgh. All S.value exceed 100. Projecting id,city gives (100,Edinburgh),(100,London),(200,Oxford),(400,London),(500,Edinburgh). Skip unmatched R keys 300,600,700. The simplified source pseudocode assumes no duplicates in R; the group version above also preserves a×b matches when both sides repeat a key.

PDF pp. 16–29

Sort-merge I/O and fused final passes

Let Csort(X)=2X[1+ceil(logB−1ceil(X/B))] for the fully materialised nonempty sort. A normal merge scan adds M+N when duplicate groups do not force rereads. With B=100, sorting source R/S costs 4000 and 2000, then merging costs 1500: total 7500 I/Os.

If the final R and S sort runs together fit the merge-input budget B−1, fuse final sorting with join matching. Read/write initial runs costs 2(M+N); final reads cost M+N, total 4500. Large repeated-key groups may spill or rescan, with a nested-loop-like worst case; “linear merge” assumes their memory/replay handling is feasible. Existing order or required ordered output makes merge joins attractive.

PDF pp. 30–33

sections.title: Hash join and algorithm choice
sections.html:
In-memory hash build and probe

H = empty multimap
for r in build R: H[hash(r.key)].append(r)
for s in probe S:
  for r in H[hash(s.key)]:
    if r.key == s.key: emit(r,s)

Store all records for a repeated key, not one record per key. A hash collision only produces a candidate. If the complete build table fits the usable memory budget, both inputs are read once: M+N. The smaller input is commonly built, but its tuple widths and hash-table overhead matter.

PDF pp. 34–35

Grace partitioning and recursion

Partition R and S with the same join-key hash into paired Rᵢ,Sᵢ. Every possible match lands in one pair, so no cross-partition comparison is needed. For each pair, build a table on its smaller side and probe the other using a suitable local hash.

Reading and writing both inputs during partitioning costs 2(M+N). Reading them for build/probe adds M+N, yielding 3(M+N)=4500 I/Os for the source. Oversized build partitions require another partitioning level or a fallback, adding I/O. Skew and repeated identical keys can defeat the even-partition assumption; they need handling rather than an automatic 4500 claim.

PDF pp. 36–40

Choosing a complete join implementation

Compare predicate support, existing indexes/order, build memory, input asymmetry and output needs. Nested loops supports arbitrary conditions; indexed NL exploits selective matching access; sort-merge exploits useful order; hashing exploits equality and a small build side.

The source timing table assumes 0.1 ms per I/O and omits CPU/output consistently. It is a comparison under those assumptions, not a benchmark ranking. Sorting avoids hash-distribution sensitivity but still has duplicate/output-size costs; hashing does not magically remove many-to-many output.

PDF pp. 41–43

quiz.question: Two groups with the same key contain 3 and 4 tuples. How many joined tuples do they produce?
quiz.explanation: Pair each of the three first-input occurrences with all four second-input occurrences: 4+4+4=12 output tuples. A join does not deduplicate the groups. Sorting or hashing can organise the comparisons differently, but cannot discard any of these valid pairs.
